title: Biochemistry
tagline: Water and weak bonds, the molecules of life, enzymes, bioenergetics and the central pathways of metabolism
summary: Living things run on chemistry: a few kinds of molecule, folded and assembled, catalyse and regulate thousands of reactions. This course covers water and weak interactions, proteins, carbohydrates, lipids and nucleotides, enzyme kinetics and regulation, bioenergetics, and the central pathways of metabolism, from glycolysis to oxidative phosphorylation, and how they are controlled.
overview: Biochemistry is the study of life as chemistry: how a few kinds of molecule — water, amino acids, sugars, lipids and nucleotides — are assembled into the proteins, membranes, stores and genes of a cell, and how thousands of enzyme-catalysed reactions are organised into pathways that extract energy from food or light, build new cells and keep the whole system far from equilibrium. It underlies every other part of biology, from the physiology of a sprinting muscle or a hibernating squirrel to the ecology of anaerobic sediments and the yield of a maize field, and it is the basis of medicine, nutrition, agriculture and biotechnology.

The course is written from the biologist's side. It begins with water, pH and the weak interactions that hold biological molecules together, inside real compartments and in organisms that live in the deep sea, in deserts and under ice; then treats proteins, carbohydrates, lipids and nucleotides as products of evolution with jobs to do; enzymes, their kinetics in the cell, their isozymes and their adaptation to temperature; the regulation of enzymes and the question of who controls a pathway's flux; bioenergetics in cells and whole organisms; glycolysis, the diversity of fermentations and the citric acid cycle; oxidative phosphorylation, chemiosmosis, uncoupling for heat and respiration without oxygen; and finally the integration of metabolism across tissues, through feeding and fasting, and in C4 and CAM plants. The detailed chemistry of mechanisms and the thermodynamic derivations are in the biochemistry course of Chemistry Atlas, to which the lessons link; clinical biochemistry belongs to Medicine Atlas.

Metabolism can look like an endless wall chart of names. The way through is to ask a few questions of every pathway — which way does it run and why (free energy and mass-action ratios), how fast and who controls it (kinetics, allostery and control coefficients), what does it cost and what does it yield (ATP, NADH and NADPH), where is it (compartments and tissues) and how did it come to be (comparative and evolutionary evidence) — and to check the answers with numbers. Each lesson therefore works through quantitative examples verified against Berg, Nelson and Cox, Voet and Voet and the primary literature, and tells how the key experiments were done and by whom.
outcomes: Explain how hydrogen bonds, the hydrophobic effect and other weak interactions determine biological structure and binding, and relate binding free energy to dissociation constants.
Calculate pH, buffer behaviour, ion trapping and osmotic pressure in biological compartments, and interpret how organisms use compatible osmolytes and pH regulation to live in extreme environments.
Describe the structures and biological roles of proteins, carbohydrates, lipids and nucleotides, and interpret data from protein methods such as SDS-PAGE and mass spectrometry.

Analyse enzyme kinetic data using the Michaelis–Menten equation, specificity constants and inhibition models, and relate kinetic parameters to physiological substrate concentrations, isozymes and temperature adaptation.
Explain allosteric regulation, cooperativity and covalent modification, and use metabolic control analysis to reason about which enzymes control a pathway's flux.
Calculate actual free-energy changes, energy charge and redox potentials in cells, and estimate ATP turnover and metabolic rate from oxygen consumption.
Trace the flow of carbon and electrons through glycolysis, fermentations and the citric acid cycle, balance fermentation equations, and explain the trade-off between the rate and yield of ATP.
Explain the chemiosmotic mechanism of oxidative phosphorylation, calculate proton-motive force and P/O ratios, and interpret oxygen-electrode and inhibitor experiments.
Describe how fuel use is divided among tissues and switched between feeding, fasting and starvation by hormones, and interpret respiratory quotients and nitrogen-excretion strategies comparatively.
Compare metabolic adaptations across organisms, including anoxia tolerance, thermogenesis, C4 and CAM photosynthesis, and the glyoxylate cycle, and evaluate the evidence for their evolution.

history.title: Cell-free fermentation
history.detail: Eduard Buchner showed that juice pressed from ground yeast, with no living cells, ferments sugar to ethanol and CO₂, proving that the chemistry of life can be studied outside the cell.

history.title: Michaelis–Menten kinetics
history.detail: Leonor Michaelis and Maud Menten measured initial rates of sucrose hydrolysis by yeast invertase and explained their saturation by an enzyme–substrate complex.

history.title: The urea cycle
history.detail: Working with rat liver slices, Hans Krebs and Kurt Henseleit found that ornithine catalytically stimulates urea synthesis — the first metabolic cycle to be described.

history.title: The citric acid cycle
history.detail: Using minced pigeon breast muscle and the inhibitor malonate, Krebs and William Arthur Johnson showed that citrate is formed from oxaloacetate and acts catalytically, joining known reactions into a cycle.

history.title: ATP as the energy currency
history.detail: Fritz Lipmann's review introduced the 'energy-rich phosphate bond' and the idea that ATP links energy-releasing and energy-consuming reactions throughout metabolism.

history.title: The photosynthetic carbon cycle
history.detail: By exposing the alga Chlorella to ¹⁴CO₂ for seconds and separating the labelled products, Melvin Calvin, Andrew Benson and James Bassham worked out the cycle by which Rubisco fixes CO₂, completing it in the mid-1950s.

history.title: Regulatory phosphorylation
history.detail: Edmond Fischer and Edwin Krebs showed that conversion of rabbit-muscle glycogen phosphorylase from its b to its a form requires ATP and a kinase, discovering reversible protein phosphorylation.

history.title: The chemiosmotic hypothesis
history.detail: Peter Mitchell proposed that respiration and photosynthesis make ATP through a proton gradient across a membrane, rather than through a high-energy chemical intermediate.

history.title: The concerted model of allostery
history.detail: Jacques Monod, Jeffries Wyman and Jean-Pierre Changeux explained cooperative binding and allosteric regulation by a concerted transition between two conformations of a symmetric oligomer.

history.title: ATP synthase seen rotating
history.detail: Hiroyuki Noji, Masasuke Yoshida, Kazuhiko Kinosita and colleagues attached an actin filament to the γ subunit of bacterial F₁-ATPase and watched it rotate in 120° steps as ATP was hydrolysed.

references.title: Lehninger Principles of Biochemistry
references.authors: David L. Nelson and Michael M. Cox
references.note: 8th edition. The standard undergraduate text: clear on metabolism, its regulation and integration, with good data-analysis problems.

references.title: Biochemistry
references.authors: Jeremy M. Berg, John L. Tymoczko, Gregory J. Gatto Jr. and Lubert Stryer
references.note: 10th edition. Strong on enzyme mechanisms, structure and the experimental basis of each topic; excellent figures.

references.title: Biochemistry
references.authors: Donald Voet and Judith G. Voet
references.note: 4th edition. The most detailed of the general texts; the place to look up mechanisms, kinetics and thermodynamics in depth.

references.title: Biochemistry
references.authors: Reginald H. Garrett and Charles M. Grisham
references.note: 6th edition. A thorough alternative to the above with a clear treatment of metabolic pathways and their control.

references.title: Biochemical Adaptation: Mechanism and Process in Physiological Evolution
references.authors: Peter W. Hochachka and George N. Somero
references.note: The classic account of how enzymes, osmolytes and pathways are adapted to temperature, pressure, oxygen and water across animals.

references.title: Bioenergetics 4
references.authors: David G. Nicholls and Stuart J. Ferguson
references.note: The standard monograph on chemiosmosis, respiratory chains, ATP synthase and photosynthetic energy transduction.

references.title: Understanding the Control of Metabolism
references.note: A readable introduction to metabolic control analysis and why rate-limiting steps are rare.

references.title: Human Metabolism: A Regulatory Perspective
references.authors: Keith N. Frayn and Rhys D. Evans
references.note: 4th edition. Integration of metabolism across human tissues in feeding, fasting and exercise, from a physiologist's viewpoint.
